The dialogue survives in Vanderbilt's retrospective account of May 3, 1866, not a contemporary transcript. These are same-year visual references; the photograph does not establish his March 17 clothing or that he wore a hat indoors. looks.look: Born December 19, 1814; age calculated for the episode. Vanderbilt University's account describes rounded shoulders, receding slicked-back hair, small round glasses and a gray beard without a moustache. Its stated age of 46 is inconsistent with Stanton's documented birth date. Mississippi State's Brady portrait independently documents his glasses. Exact meeting clothes are not established by these sources. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/people/edwin-m-stanton.htm?ms=nav&utm_source=openai))

looks.look: The National Park Service identifies Georgian and neoclassical influences in James Hoban's design. The Library of Congress's March 1861 photograph records the north front, with a Thomas Jefferson statue on the lawn and the conservatory to the right. Vanderbilt's account identifies the mansion but not the meeting room: no particular room, desk, furniture arrangement or wall decoration is verified for this encounter. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/places/white-house.htm?utm_source=openai))

The archived U.S. Naval Historical Center page describes a wooden, side-wheel steamship originally built for transatlantic passenger service. Its captions identify two funnels and supply a Civil War photograph, NH 42188, plus an 1862 engraving, NH 58744. The consulted text does not specify her sailing rig; do not substitute the full sailing rig she received after conversion into Three Brothers in 1873. ([ibiblio.org](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/OnlineLibrary/photos/sh-usn/usnsh-v/vanderbt.htm))

looks.look: A casemate ironclad ram, not a turreted monitor. The Smithsonian describes construction from the salvaged hull of USS Merrimack, with wood covered by layers of sheet iron and ten guns; its collection model supplies a documented shape reference. This vessel is background to the meeting, not a ship Vanderbilt actually sinks in this episode. ([civilwar.si.edu](https://civilwar.si.edu/navies_cssvirginia.html?utm_source=openai))

looks.look: The Virginia Department of Historic Resources documents an irregular Third System fortification of brick and masonry: seven fronts, large bastions, five-foot-thick walls and a surrounding wet moat. facts.fact: Stanton escorted Vanderbilt to the Executive Mansion in Washington to meet Lincoln, according to Vanderbilt's later account. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000/pdf/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000.pdf))

Vanderbilt said he and Lincoln had not previously been personally acquainted. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000/pdf/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000.pdf))

Lincoln asked whether Vanderbilt's steamships could prevent the Confederate Merrimac from leaving Hampton Roads. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000/pdf/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000.pdf))

Vanderbilt claimed his properly manned steamship Vanderbilt could deter the ironclad—or had ten-to-one odds of destroying her. This was his prediction, not a battle result. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000/pdf/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000.pdf))

Lincoln then asked Vanderbilt to name his price for undertaking the service. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000/pdf/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000.pdf))

Vanderbilt refused to profit from the government's emergency and offered the ship outright as a gift instead of naming a charter price. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000/pdf/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000.pdf))

Vanderbilt recalled Lincoln answering, “I accept her.” He said the equipped ship reached Fortress Monroe within the promised three or four days. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000/pdf/SERIALSET-01238_00_00-021-0046-0000.pdf))

Lincoln independently confirmed to Congress that Vanderbilt had given the United States the steamer in March. He reported that she was already performing valuable government service and recommended a suitable acknowledgment. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-01123_00_00-007-0071-0000/pdf/SERIALSET-01123_00_00-007-0071-0000.pdf?utm_source=openai))

story.story:
On March 17, 1862, Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton escorts Cornelius Vanderbilt to the Executive Mansion in Washington to meet Abraham Lincoln. Vanderbilt and Lincoln have not previously been personally acquainted, as Vanderbilt recalled on May 3, 1866.

Lincoln asks whether Vanderbilt’s steamships can prevent the Confederate Merrimac from leaving Hampton Roads. Vanderbilt claims that his steamship Vanderbilt, properly manned, could deter the ironclad—or have ten-to-one odds of destroying her. He is making a prediction, not describing a victory.

Lincoln asks Vanderbilt to name his price for undertaking the service. Vanderbilt refuses to profit from the government’s emergency: instead of naming a charter price, he offers the ship outright as a gift. Lincoln answers, as Vanderbilt later recalled, “I accept her.”
story.title: I Accept Her
